content: The examination of patients with peritonitis often reveals signs of an acute abdomen. In advanced cases, signs of shock and septicemia may also be present. Physical Examination General Appearance Patients with peritonitis typically appear unwell. Initially, they may seem alert, restless, and irritable. As the condition progresses, they may become apathetic and delirious. They are often observed lying quietly in a supine position with their knees flexed. This posture minimizes movement, as any motion exacerbates abdominal pain. Their breathing is frequently shallow and limited to intercostal respiration due to the pain. Vital Signs Temperature Hyperthermia, with temperatures reaching as high as 42°C, is indicative of infection. Hypothermia, with temperatures as low as 35°C, suggests septic shock. Hypothermia is a particularly ominous sign, often occurring late in the disease course in patients with ongoing intra-abdominal sepsis or septic shock. Blood Pressure Hypertension may occur if there is an associated cardiac or renal condition. Blood pressure is typically maintained within normal limits during the early stages of the disease. However, as peritonitis progresses, blood pressure decreases due to volume loss, diarrhea, or severe ascites. Pulse Tachycardia with weak, thready peripheral pulses indicates reduced effective circulating blood volume, a hallmark of shock in the later stages of the disease. The pulse rate may be normal or elevated due to infection. A low pulse volume may be observed in cases of dehydration. Respiration Tachypnea is often present, driven by infection and increased metabolic demand. Skin The abdominal skin may appear tense due to ascites. Skin changes such as spider nevi, palmar erythema, and prominent abdominal wall collateral veins suggest parenchymal liver disease and portal hypertension. Eyes Jaundice may be observed in cases of liver cirrhosis. Periorbital puffiness may be noted in patients with renal failure. Neck Jugular venous distension may be present in cases of heart failure leading to ascites. Heart Signs of heart failure, such as an S3 gallop, may be detected. Lungs Evidence of infection or signs of pulmonary volume overload due to heart failure may be present. Neurologic Findings In cases of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or underlying liver or renal failure, the following neurologic symptoms may be observed: Stupor Confusion Seizures Abdomen The abdomen is usually tense and distended due to ascites. Marked abdominal tenderness is present on palpation. Shifting dullness on percussion is noted in patients with ascites, though this may be painful if infection is present. Bowel sounds vary during the course of peritonitis. Initially, they may be hypoactive and can disappear entirely in later stages. In some patients, the absence of bowel sounds may be the only indication of peritonitis, necessitating a high index of suspicion. The absence of any of these findings does not rule out peritonitis. Extremities Peripheral edema, when present in patients with liver disease, is typically found in the lower extremities and may occasionally involve the abdominal wall. Patients with nephrotic syndrome or cardiac failure may exhibit generalized body edema (anasarca).
